blocks.title: Buffer solution
blocks.text: Solutions that resist a change in their pH when a small amount of an acid or a base is added to them are called buffer solutions. They have a specific constant pH, and their pH does not change on dilution or on keeping for a long time.

Buffer solutions are mostly prepared by mixing two substances. Mixing a weak acid with its salt with a strong base gives an acidic buffer with pH less than 7; acetic acid with sodium acetate is one of the best examples. Mixing a weak base with its salt with a strong acid gives a basic buffer with pH more than 7; NH4OH with NH4Cl is one of the best examples.

Consider the acidic buffer of CH3COOH and CH3COONa. Acetic acid, a weak electrolyte, dissociates very little: CH3COOH(aq) + H2O(l) gives CH3COO-(aq) + H3O+(aq). When sodium acetate, a strong electrolyte, is added, CH3COONa(aq) gives CH3COO-(aq) + Na+(aq), the dissociation of CH3COOH is suppressed by the common ion effect of CH3COO-. As more CH3COONa is added, the added acetate decreases the dissociation of CH3COOH and the pH of the solution increases; the greater the concentration of acetic acid compared with sodium acetate, the lower the pH. Table 9.4 shows how the pH of the mixture is maintained.

blocks.long_description: Adding an ion that an equilibrium already produces pushes that equilibrium back: chloride from HCl precipitates NaCl from brine, and acetate ions cut the dissociation of acetic acid from 1.3 per cent to 0.012 per cent while the pH rises from 2.89 to 4.92. The resulting mixture is a buffer: added H3O+ is taken up by acetate and added OH- by acetic acid, so the pH hardly moves, and Henderson's equation gives that pH as pKa plus the logarithm of the salt-to-acid ratio, equal to pKa (4.74) when the two are equal. For sparingly soluble salts the same idea becomes the solubility product: Ksp is the product of the ion concentrations raised to their coefficients, it fixes the solubility (1.18 x 10^-2 mol dm-3 for calcium hydroxide), a common ion lowers that solubility, and a salt precipitates only when the ionic product exceeds Ksp.

blocks.text: A buffer of this kind is a large reservoir of CH3COOH and CH3COO-. When an acid (H3O+ ions) is added, the ions react with CH3COO- to give back acetic acid, so the pH remains almost unchanged, because CH3COOH, a weak acid, prefers to remain undissociated. Similarly the buffer of NH4Cl and NH4OH resists a change of pH and pOH when acid or base is added from outside. When a base (OH- ions) is added, the ions react with H3O+ to give back H2O and the pH again remains almost unchanged.

blocks.prompt: Explain how the acetate buffer resists the addition of a few drops of NaOH, and of a few drops of HCl.
blocks.explanation: Added OH- reacts with the undissociated acetic acid in the reservoir, CH3COOH + OH- giving CH3COO- + H2O, so the hydroxide is consumed instead of raising the pH. Added H+ reacts with the acetate ions, CH3COO- + H+ giving CH3COOH, so the acid is consumed instead of lowering the pH. Only the ratio of acid to acetate changes slightly, and the pH shifts very little.

items: Buffers resist pH change on adding a little acid or base and on dilution: acidic buffer = weak acid + its salt (CH3COOH / CH3COONa, pH below 7); basic buffer = weak base + its salt (NH4OH / NH4Cl, pH above 7).
Acetate suppresses acetic acid's dissociation (Table 9.4: 1.3 to 0.012 per cent, pH 2.89 to 4.92); added H3O+ is removed by CH3COO-, added OH- by CH3COOH.
